newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka military closer to marginalising rebels.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka military closer to marginalising rebels.

text.p: Sri Lanka's military has suffered several setbacks in its campaign against Tamil Tiger rebels during the last three years, but military analysts say it is now closer than ever to marginalising the guerrillas.

The military's achievements can be largely attributed to President Chandrika Kumaratunga, who as defence minister has equipped the soldiers better and provided political leadership that has encouraged troops to fight the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE), analysts said.
Kumaratunga's People's Alliance government completed three years in power on Saturday.

"On the whole, the prospects are looking better for the military. They are better equipped and fighting to a plan, but people will have to be patient," said General Dennis Perera, a retired army commander.
But the accomplishments come with heavy casualties on both sides, and the war has intensified with the rebels using artillery taken during attacks on military camps.

"The war has escalated during the last three years, it has become of a higher intensity. But we have achieved a lot in territory as well as tactically," said military spokesman Brigadier Sarath Munasinghe.

The conflict has also had a big, although not a crippling, effect on the economy. The government's defence budget has risen sharply and there are vast areas in the north where there is little economic activity as thousands of displaced people try to find a livelihood.
LTTE rebels are fighting a 14-year-old war for a separate homeland for minority Tamils in predominately Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east.
The government says more than 50,000 people have died in the fighting. The LTTE claim the figure is higher.

Kumaratunga's People's Alliance was voted into power in August 1994, ending the 17-year rule of the United National Party (UNP), during which the military made certain advances but often had to back-pedal to consolidate their positions.
Kumaratunga changed this.

After a brief round of peace talks, which ended when the guerrillas blew up two naval gunaboats in the northeastern port town of Trincomalee in early 1995, Kumaratunga set the military on a campaign to take the rebels head-on.
The military unfolded a new strategy, going after the rebels in their long-time stronghold of the northern Jaffna peninsula.

By mid 1996, troops managed to drive the rebels out of the peninsula, and when the guerrillas set up new headquarters at Kilinochchi, a town in the northern Wanni region, the soldiers went after them there.
Early this year, troops captured a highway from the frontier northern town of Vavuniya to northwestern Mannar, and since then have been on a campaign to open the vital road to Jaffna.
"Taking the highway from Vavuniya to Jaffna is very significant, but to hold it means committing a huge number of troops," said Harry Goonatilleke, a retired air force chief.

Critics say the military achievement in the north has been at the expense of conceeding the east to the rebels. Even in the north the troops have stretched themselves by holding onto large swathes of land that makes them vulnerable to rebel attacks.
"More than a dozen soldiers are killed almost every fortnight in Jaffna. This is the price we have to pay for holding the land," said Goonatilleke.

But Munasinghe said that despite the limited resources, troops have developed certain tactics to hold the north, while in the east the soldiers are in command of the main towns and highways where most people live.
"Clearing the east will be a matter of weeks if we have the correct quantum of troops on the ground," he said.
But this could be a problem as recruitment campaigns during the past few years have received little response, prompting the military to go after thousands of deserters.
The military's recent achievements may have prompted Kumaratunga's prediction of an early end to the war, threatening to wipe out the rebels in the process if needed.
"If we have to defeat them, we will do so," she told a passing-out parade of army officers in Colombo last week.
But Foreign Minister Lakshman Kadirgamar seems more realistic.

"We cannot eliminate every single terrorist. What we want to do is to hit the LTTE to such an extent that it will no longer be the formidable fighting machine that it has been allowed to become in this last decade," Kadirgamar told Germany's Handelsblatt newspaper in a recent interview.
